806.title: Baba Buddha
806.hook: the boy Nanak met lived to serve six Gurus and, tradition says, applied the tilak to their successors
806.howItsDone: Sikhs honor Baba Buddha as a model of lifelong seva, and gurdwaras connected with his memory, including Gurdwara Bir Baba Buddha Sahib, draw visitors who come to remember his service.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mata Khivi, named in the Granth: shade like a leafy tree, kheer made with ghee. Your line was generous kitchen. Did something you made go a little further? Day eight hundred six.

A boy is out with the cattle when a holy man passes by on the road. He could have kept his eyes on the herd. Instead he brings milk, sits down, and asks a question that sounds far too old for him. How do I escape death? The holy man looks at him and asks why a boy so young is thinking about that. The boy's answer, as Sikhs tell it, earned him a new name for the rest of his life. Today: Baba Buddha.
screen: `A BOY WITH THE CATTLE.` → `A QUESTION ABOUT DEATH.` → `AN ANSWER THAT EARNED A NAME.`

segments.voice: The story comes from Sikh tradition, and it goes like this. The boy, named Bura, tells Guru Nanak what he saw at home. When his mother lights the cooking fire, she doesn't start with the big logs. She starts with the small twigs, and they burn up first. So, he says, if the small ones go first in the fire, who's to say death will wait for the old? Guru Nanak, the story says, answered that he spoke like an old man, a buddha, a wise elder. And the name stuck: Baba Buddha. Then comes the long part. That boy, tradition says, lived to serve six Gurus, from Guru Nanak on. When guruship passed from one Guru to the next, tradition says it was Baba Buddha who applied the tilak, the mark on the forehead, to the new Guru. The same pair of hands that once herded cattle by the road marked Guru after Guru, across a lifetime. And Sikh tradition remembers him at the Harmandir Sahib too: when Guru Arjan installed the Granth there, tradition says Baba Buddha was asked to read from it. Through all of it, the stories don't make him a leader who sought power. He's honored for service. He tended, he read, he marked, he stayed. His question as a boy was how to escape death. The name came first, from a boy watching twigs catch in his mother's fire. The long life of service came after, and Sikhs remember the two together: a child who spoke like an elder, and an elder who kept serving like that same attentive boy, one Guru after another.
screen: `SMALL TWIGS BURN FIRST.` · `A BOY CALLED BUDDHA: A WISE ELDER.` · `THE TILAK, GURU AFTER GURU.` · `HONORED FOR SERVICE, NOT POWER.` · then, large: `SIX GURUS SERVED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: serve for the long haul. In the sit, bring to mind one thing you could keep doing for a long time: a weekly call, a small job at a gurdwara or a community place, a way you help at home. Not something heroic. Something you could still be doing years from now. Hold it with each breath, and let it feel ordinary. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Baba Buddha. The boy whose question about death earned him the name of a wise elder, and who, tradition says, served six Gurus and marked their successors with the tilak.
Your line: six gurus served. Today, do the one small service you could keep doing for years, and do it once with care. Day eight hundred six.

807.title: Bibi Amro
807.hook: Guru Angad's daughter whose dawn singing brought Amar Das to the Guru
807.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Bibi Amro in the story of how Guru Amar Das came to Guru Angad, and some Sikh households still sing gurbani during ordinary work, at home and at dawn.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Baba Buddha, the boy who met Guru Nanak and, tradition says, lived long enough to serve one Guru after another. Your line was six gurus served. Did someone's long faithfulness come to mind? Today, a song before sunrise. Day eight hundred seven.

It's still dark. In a village house a young woman sits at the churn, pulling the cord back and forth, turning milk into butter the way it was done every morning. And while her hands work, she sings. Not loudly. Just enough to keep time with the churn. On the other side of the wall, an older man in the same family is awake too. He's a devout man, and tradition says he has walked to the holy river many times in his life, still looking for something. He hears the words. He stops what he's doing. And he asks a question that will change the rest of his life: whose words are these? Today: Bibi Amro.
screen: `STILL DARK, A CHURN, A SONG.` → `AN OLDER MAN LISTENING.` → `WHOSE WORDS ARE THESE?`

segments.voice: Bibi Amro was the daughter of Guru Angad, the second Guru, who sat in Guru Nanak's seat at Khadur. Tradition says she married into the family of a man named Amar Das, and went to live in his village. Amar Das was religious in the way of his time. He kept fasts, he went on pilgrimage, he was good and careful. But the story says he had never had a teacher. Then, one morning, he heard his young relative singing at her work. The song was a hymn of Guru Nanak. Tradition says the words went straight into him. He came to her and asked whose they were. She told him plainly: these are Guru Nanak's words, and my father now sits in his place. That's all she had to say. Amar Das asked her to take him there. So she did. She brought him to Khadur, to her father, and he never really left. The story says he stayed to serve Guru Angad, carrying water, doing the plain work of the house, for years. And in time, Guru Angad chose him to be the next Guru. Guru Amar Das, the third Guru. Now notice what Bibi Amro did, and what she didn't. She didn't argue with him. She didn't set out to convince anybody. She was churning butter. The song was part of her morning, as ordinary as the milk. And because it was real to her, it carried through a wall. Some people share what they believe by arguing for it. Sikhs remember Bibi Amro for sharing it the other way: it simply sounded while she worked. One woman, singing at dawn, and the Guruship found its next keeper.
screen: `A DAUGHTER OF GURU ANGAD.` · `A HYMN SUNG WHILE CHURNING.` · `TAKE ME TO YOUR FATHER.` · `FAITH THAT CARRIES THROUGH A WALL.` · then, large: `HER SONG CHANGED A LIFE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sing something near someone. Not a performance. Just a quiet song while you do something with your hands. For this sit, start by settling. Let the breath find its own pace. Bring to mind one song or line you love, sacred or not. If you know a shabad, you can use that. Let it run quietly in your head, in time with the breath, the way Bibi Amro kept time with the churn. After the bell, if someone is nearby, hum it softly while you wash a cup or fold something. The bell holds the time.
Bibi Amro. Guru Angad's daughter, whose song at dawn, tradition says, brought Amar Das to the Guru. Today's word.

Your line: her song changed a life. Today, let something you love be heard in an ordinary moment, a hum in the kitchen, a line said aloud, without trying to make it mean anything. Day eight hundred seven.

808.title: Bibi Bhani
808.hook: daughter of one Guru, wife of another, mother of a third; tradition says she once held her father's stool steady with her hand
808.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Bibi Bhani as the daughter of Guru Amar Das, wife of Guru Ram Das and mother of Guru Arjan, and tell the story of the broken stool as an example of quiet, steady service.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bibi Amro sang at the churn, and Amar Das heard Guru Nanak's words through the wall. Your line was her song changed a life. Did you let something you love be heard? Today, Guru Amar Das's own daughter. Day eight hundred eight.

A low wooden stool. Short legs, a flat seat, the kind of thing every household had and nobody looked at twice. Tradition says Guru Amar Das sat on one like it each morning while he bathed and prayed. And one morning, a leg gave way. Nobody in the story makes a speech. Nobody calls for a carpenter. His daughter is there, and she does the only thing there's time to do. She slides her hand under the broken corner and holds the seat level, so her father's stillness isn't broken. Today: Bibi Bhani.
screen: `A LOW WOODEN STOOL.` → `ONE LEG GIVES WAY.` → `A HAND UNDER THE CORNER.`

segments.voice: Bibi Bhani's family tree reads like a list of the Gurus themselves. She was the daughter of Guru Amar Das, the third Guru. She married Bhai Jetha, a young man from Lahore who served in her father's house, and he became Guru Ram Das, the fourth. And their son became Guru Arjan, the fifth. Daughter of one Guru, wife of another, mother of a third. Now the stool. Tradition tells it this way. The leg broke while her father sat in prayer, and Bibi Bhani put her hand beneath the seat and held it. She held it so long, the story says, that the wood cut her hand and it bled. She didn't move, and she didn't call out. When Guru Amar Das opened his eyes, he saw the blood on the floor and understood what had happened. Tradition says he was moved, and told her to ask for something. And what she asked for wasn't jewelry, or rest, or praise. She asked that the Guruship stay in her household. Sikh tradition reads what followed through that moment: from her husband onward, the Gurus came from her family line. Some tellings say her father warned her that the gift would come with suffering, and Sikhs remember that it did. So the story holds two things at once. It's about devotion that doesn't need an audience. And it's about steadiness as a kind of strength. Holding something level is quiet work. Nobody claps for it. But a whole household, and in this story a whole line of Gurus, can rest on a hand that doesn't let go.
screen: `DAUGHTER, WIFE AND MOTHER OF GURUS.` · `SHE HELD THE STOOL UNTIL IT BLED.` · `SHE ASKED FOR THE GURUSHIP TO STAY.` · `STEADINESS NOBODY CLAPS FOR.` · then, large: `SHE HELD IT STEADY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: steady something for someone. First, steady yourself. Settle, and let the breath find its own pace. Rest one hand, palm up, on your knee, as if something small were sitting on it. Feel how much attention it takes to keep a hand still. Then think of one person in your life who is carrying something heavy right now. What could you hold level for them today? A ride, a meal, an hour of quiet, an errand. Hold that one thing in mind with your steady hand. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Bibi Bhani. Daughter of Guru Amar Das, wife of Guru Ram Das, mother of Guru Arjan, who, tradition says, held her father's stool steady with her own hand. Today's word.
Your line: she held it steady. Today, do the one steadying thing you thought of in the sit, without mentioning it, and let it be enough that it held. Day eight hundred eight.

809.title: Mata Ganga
809.hook: Guru Arjan's wife, who, tradition says, walked to Baba Buddha with simple bread and onions to ask for a son's blessing
809.howItsDone: Sikhs tell the story of Mata Ganga's visit to Baba Buddha as a lesson in humility: the blessing came when she walked there with bread she had made herself.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bibi Bhani held her father's broken stool level until her hand bled. Your line was she held it steady. What did you hold level for someone? Today, her daughter-in-law. Day eight hundred nine.

What do you bring to someone whose blessing you want? One instinct is to bring the best we have. The good dishes. The nicest clothes. A little ceremony, to show we mean it. That's exactly what Mata Ganga did the first time. Tradition says she set out with attendants and a carriage and fine food, to visit an old man who lived out among the fields and cattle. And she came home with nothing. The second time, she walked. Today: Mata Ganga.
screen: `WHAT DO YOU BRING?` → `THE FIRST TIME: CARRIAGE AND FINE FOOD.` → `THE SECOND TIME: SHE WALKED.`

segments.voice: Mata Ganga was the wife of Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, Bibi Bhani's son. Tradition says that for a long time the couple had no child, and Mata Ganga longed for a son. Guru Arjan, the story goes, sent her to Baba Buddha, the old Sikh who had known Guru Nanak and now tended the Guru's fields and herds. So she went the way a Guru's wife might be expected to go: with a carriage, with servants, with rich dishes. The dust of the procession rolled up the road. And Baba Buddha, tradition says, asked what all the commotion was about, and gave no blessing. She went home disappointed. Guru Arjan didn't scold her. He suggested another way. This time she ground the flour and kneaded the dough herself. She made plain bread, the kind farm workers eat, and took onions and buttermilk with it. And she went on foot, alone or nearly so, carrying it. When she reached Baba Buddha, he was hungry from the work, and he was glad. He sat and ate. And then, tradition says, he took an onion and crushed it in his fist, and said that her son would be strong enough to crush the pride of tyrants the same way. Sikhs say the son born to her was Guru Hargobind, the Guru remembered for taking up the sword alongside the Name. So what changed between the first visit and the second? Not the request. Not the person. Only how she came. With the carriage, she arrived as someone important. With the bread, she arrived as someone asking. The story says the blessing waited for the second.
screen: `A LONGING FOR A SON.` · `THE CARRIAGE: NO BLESSING.` · `PLAIN BREAD, ON FOOT.` · `AN ONION CRUSHED IN HIS FIST.` · then, large: `SIMPLE BREAD, BIG BLESSING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take someone a simple meal. For this sit, start by settling. Let the breath find its own pace. Then bring to mind one person who could use something plain and warm today. Not a gift to impress. A sandwich, a bowl of soup, tea in a flask, fruit you washed yourself. Let the picture be specific: what you'd carry, how you'd get there, where you'd set it down. Notice any urge to make it fancier, and let it go. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Mata Ganga. Guru Arjan's wife and, Sikhs say, Guru Hargobind's mother, who went back to Baba Buddha on foot with bread she made herself. Today's word.
Your line: simple bread, big blessing. Today, make or bring one plain thing for someone, by your own hands if you can, and deliver it without ceremony. Day eight hundred nine.

810.title: Bhai Gurdas, the man
810.hook: the scribe who, tradition says, was once tested and forgiven by Guru Hargobind
810.howItsDone: Sikhs honor Bhai Gurdas as the scribe of the Granth and the author of the Vars, which are sung in gurdwaras, and they tell the story of his test and forgiveness as part of who he was.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mata Ganga walked to Baba Buddha with bread she'd made herself. Your line was simple bread, big blessing. Did a plain meal reach someone? Today, a man the path has met before, seen up close. Day eight hundred ten.

A letter arrives at a king's court in Banaras, far from Punjab. It's from Guru Hargobind, and it says something strange. A thief of mine is hiding in your city. Find him, tie his hands, and send him back to me. The king's men go looking. And before they find anyone, a quiet, learned man steps forward and says: that's me. I'm the one he means. The thief is the Guru's own scribe. Today: Bhai Gurdas, the man.
screen: `A LETTER TO BANARAS.` → `FIND MY THIEF AND TIE HIS HANDS.` → `THAT'S ME.`

segments.voice: Bhai Gurdas is a name this path has met as a writer. Tradition says he wrote out the Granth as Guru Arjan dictated it, and Sikhs speak of his own Vars as a key to the Guru's word. So it's a surprise that the story Sikhs tell about him as a man is a story of failure. Tradition tells it in more than one version. In a well-known one, Guru Hargobind sent him to Kabul with money to buy horses. He made the bargain, and went into his tent to fetch the payment. And the money wasn't there. Some tellings say it had turned to stones. Standing there, with the dealers waiting outside, he panicked. He was the Guru's trusted man, and he couldn't pay. So he slipped out the back of the tent and ran, all the way to Banaras, where nobody knew him. Some tellings add a reason for the test: that he had come to feel sure no true Sikh could ever waver. Then came the letter about the thief. He knew at once who was meant. He gave himself up, and was led back with his hands tied. And in front of Guru Hargobind, tradition says, he answered in verse: admitting he had failed, and asking for mercy the way a child asks a parent. The Guru forgave him, and he stayed in the Guru's house until the end of his life. Here's what's striking. Sikhs didn't hide this story to protect a great name. They kept it. The man tradition credits with writing out the Granth was tested, ran, came back, and was forgiven. The tradition seems to want everyone to know: even he was tested.
screen: `THE SCRIBE AND POET.` · `SENT TO KABUL, THE MONEY GONE.` · `HE RAN TO BANARAS.` · `BROUGHT BACK, AND FORGIVEN.` · then, large: `EVEN HE WAS TESTED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: forgive someone's lapse. Settle, and let the breath find its own pace. Bring to mind one person who let you down in a small way recently. A late reply, a dropped promise, a moment they ran instead of facing something. Don't replay it. Just see them, the way Guru Hargobind saw a frightened man with tied hands. Notice whether you've been keeping them in the thief's role. On each breath out, loosen the knot a little. You don't have to tell them anything yet. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Bhai Gurdas. The scribe and poet who, tradition says, failed a test, ran, came back with his hands tied, and was forgiven by Guru Hargobind. Today's word.
Your line: even he was tested. Today, when someone falls short, including you, remember the Guru's scribe ran too, and let one lapse be forgiven. Day eight hundred ten.

811.title: Bhai Bidhi Chand
811.hook: a former thief turned Sikh, famous in tradition for recovering the Guru's horses from Lahore in disguise
811.howItsDone: Sikhs tell the story of Bhai Bidhi Chand as one of the companions of Guru Hargobind, remembered for his courage and cleverness after he left a life of theft and came to the Guru.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhai Gurdas ran to Banaras, came back with his hands tied, and was forgiven. Your line was even he was tested. Did you let one lapse go? Today, a man whose past was worse than one lapse. Day eight hundred eleven.

Some skills don't look good on a résumé. Moving without a sound. Reading a guard's habits. Talking your way past a gate. Getting out of a place before anyone notices you're gone. Bhai Bidhi Chand had all of them, and Sikh tradition doesn't pretend otherwise: before he came to the Guru, he was a thief. What's surprising is what happened to those skills afterward. They didn't vanish. They changed owners. Today: Bhai Bidhi Chand.
screen: `SKILLS THAT DON'T LOOK GOOD ON A RÉSUMÉ.` → `HE WAS A THIEF.` → `THE SKILLS CHANGED OWNERS.`

segments.voice: Tradition says Bidhi Chand grew up in a village near Amritsar and fell in with bad company, stealing to live. Then he came into the Guru's circle, in the time of Guru Arjan, and his life turned. He became a Sikh, and later one of Guru Hargobind's trusted companions. Now the story he's known for. Tradition says devoted Sikhs from far to the west were bringing fine horses as an offering to Guru Hargobind, and on the road, officials seized them and sent them to the royal stables in Lahore Fort. Tradition names the horses Dilbagh and Gulbagh. The Guru's people were upset. And Bidhi Chand said, in effect: leave this to me. He went to Lahore dressed as a grass-cutter. He sold the stables grass so good, and so cheap, that they hired him to tend the horses. He was patient. He won the grooms' trust. And every night, the story says, he threw a heavy stone off the fort wall into the river below, so the guards grew used to the splash and stopped looking. Then one night, the splash was him. He rode the horse over the wall into the water, swam it across, and brought it to the Guru. For the second horse, tradition says, he came back in another disguise, as a fortune-teller who claimed he could find what had been stolen, and rode off with that one too. Sikhs tell this with a grin. But under the grin is something serious. The Guru didn't ask Bidhi Chand to become a different man with no past. He took the cleverness, the nerve, the patience, and turned them toward something true.
screen: `A THIEF WHO CAME TO THE GURU.` · `THE HORSES TAKEN TO LAHORE.` · `A GRASS-CUTTER AND A NIGHTLY SPLASH.` · `OVER THE WALL, INTO THE RIVER.` · then, large: `A THIEF TURNED TRUE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: use a clever skill for good. Settle, and let the breath find its own pace. Then ask yourself, honestly: what's a skill I have that I'm a little embarrassed by? Talking people round. Finding loopholes. Noticing what others miss. Getting things done fast and not quite by the book. Don't judge it. Just name it. Then picture one way that same skill could help someone today: getting a neighbor's problem solved, untangling a form for someone, spotting what a friend needs. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Bhai Bidhi Chand. A former thief who became a Sikh and, tradition says, brought the Guru's horses back from Lahore in disguise. Today's word.
Your line: a thief turned true. Today, put the skill you named in the sit to work for someone else, once, and notice how it feels to use it in the open. Day eight hundred eleven.

812.title: Mian Mir
812.hook: a Sufi saint of Lahore who was Guru Arjan's friend; tradition says he laid the Harmandir's foundation stone
812.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Mian Mir with honor as Guru Arjan's friend, and the story that he laid the Harmandir's foundation stone is often told at the Harmandir Sahib (the Golden Temple) in Amritsar.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhai Bidhi Chand turned a thief's nerve to the Guru's service and rode a horse over the Lahore wall. Your line was a thief turned true. Did your awkward skill help someone? Today, Lahore again, and a very different man. Day eight hundred twelve.

The week ends here, so first, a roll call of the faces around the Gurus. Baba Buddha, who served Guru after Guru. Bibi Amro, singing at the churn. Bibi Bhani, her hand under a broken stool. Mata Ganga, walking with plain bread. Bhai Gurdas, the scribe who ran and came back. Bhai Bidhi Chand, over the wall. Every one of them a Sikh, or a Guru's family. And then the last face of the week, standing beside Guru Arjan at the edge of a pool in Amritsar, isn't a Sikh at all. Today: Mian Mir.
screen: `A ROLL CALL OF THE WEEK.` → `SIKHS AND THE GURUS' FAMILY.` → `THE LAST FACE ISN'T A SIKH.`

segments.voice: Mian Mir was a Sufi, a Muslim mystic, who lived in Lahore. Tradition remembers him for a plain life of prayer and for the company he kept, which included Guru Arjan. They were friends. Not allies in a debate, not rivals being polite. Friends, who visited and talked about God. Now the stone. When Guru Arjan was building the Harmandir, the house of God in the middle of the pool at Amritsar, tradition says he invited Mian Mir to lay its foundation stone. Some historians question whether it happened that way. Sikhs still tell it, and it's easy to hear why. A Sikh house of worship, with its first stone set by a Muslim friend. And that fits the building itself. The Harmandir sits low, so you step down to enter it, and it has doors on every side, open to anyone coming from any direction. There's a harder story too. When Guru Arjan was arrested and tortured in Lahore, tradition says Mian Mir came to him, grieving, and offered to intervene. And Guru Arjan, the story says, asked him not to. He told his friend that this was God's will, and that he accepted it. Mian Mir stayed a friend to the end, and the Guru stayed himself. That's the shape of this friendship. Neither man became the other. Mian Mir didn't become a Sikh. Guru Arjan didn't become a Sufi. Each stood fully in his own path, and they were close anyway. Sikhs remember Mian Mir with honor, and his shrine in Lahore is still visited. Friends across faiths, with nobody asked to switch.
screen: `A SUFI OF LAHORE.` · `TRADITION: HE LAID THE FIRST STONE.` · `DOORS ON EVERY SIDE.` · `FRIENDS TO THE HARDEST END.` · then, large: `FRIENDS ACROSS FAITHS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor a friend of another faith. Settle, and let the breath find its own pace. Bring to mind one person in your life whose path is different from yours, whether faith, or no faith, or a different way of being in the same one. See their face. Remember one time they were good to you, or good company, or just there. Let that memory sit, without trying to explain your differences. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out, and let them be in it. After the bell, you might send them a short message. The bell holds the time.
Mian Mir. A Sufi of Lahore, Guru Arjan's friend, who, tradition says, laid the foundation stone of the Harmandir. Today's word.
Your line: friends across faiths. Today, thank or honor one friend whose path isn't yours, for something specific, and don't turn it into a conversation about who's right. Day eight hundred twelve.
